title: Why Your Time-Out May Be A Waste Of Time
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin defends a full 15-minute time-out as the ideal length, pushing back against the common assumption that it's too long and will lead to boredom, restlessness, or additional misbehavior. He argues students need the first several minutes simply to calm down before they can begin the internal process of identifying what they did wrong and accepting responsibility — a progression that cannot be rushed into five or ten minutes. He connects the effectiveness of time-out directly to consistency: when consequences are delivered calmly, impersonally, and evenly across all students, the reflective process unfolds naturally and students ultimately spend less time in time-out over the course of a year. Conversely, when a student senses unfairness or personal animosity, the time-out is derailed before real reflection begins. His guidance is to state the broken rule clearly, deliver the consequence matter-of-factly, and simply walk away, letting the process do its work without any lingering emotional involvement from the teacher.
points: A full 15-minute time-out gives students enough time to move past initial upset and genuinely reflect on their mistake.
Rushing time-out to 5 or 10 minutes doesn't allow enough time for students to progress from calming down to real reflection.
Calm, consistent, impersonal delivery of consequences is what makes time-out effective, not its length.
Students who sense unfairness or personal animosity in a consequence resist reflection and misbehave more within time-out.
Delivering the consequence matter-of-factly and walking away — without lingering emotionally — allows time-out to do its work.
quotes: The thinking is that a student in time-out will miss too much participation time. They’ll grow bored and antsy and start misbehaving.
But this progression of thought doesn’t happen in five minutes. Or even 10 minutes. Your students need every bit of 15 minutes to take ownership of their mistakes.
When you enforce consequences calmly, consistently, and without causing friction, the process of reflection and responsibility comes naturally.
This is why it’s so important that time-out be as impersonal and consistent as a metronome. You’re a robot following orders, nothing more.
But length of time isn’t the problem. Students play around in time-out when they feel the consequence is unfair.
Make time-out matter to your students. Heap the responsibility for being there entirely upon their shoulders. Give them 15 minutes to stew and reflect and own up to their wrongdoing.
